draft.title: Factorising out an algebraic factor
card: Factorising is the reverse of expanding. It writes an expression as a product: a common factor multiplied by a bracket.

The highest common factor (HCF) is the largest number, pronumeral, or product of them that divides every term. For \(6x^{2}y\) and \(9xy\), the HCF is \(3xy\). For \(6x^{2}\) and \(9x\), it is \(3x\), so \(6x^{2} + 9x = 3x(2x + 3)\).
To factorise, find the HCF, write it outside the bracket, then divide each term by it to get what goes inside.

Example: \(6x^{2}y - 9xy\). The HCF is \(3xy\). \(6x^{2}y \div 3xy = 2x\) and \(9xy \div 3xy = 3\), so \(6x^{2}y - 9xy = 3xy(2x - 3)\). Expand to check: \(3xy \times 2x - 3xy \times 3 = 6x^{2}y - 9xy\).
draft.remember: Take out the HCF, then check by expanding the brackets.

a.q: Factorise \(8a^{2}b + 12ab\) by taking out the HCF.
a.why: The HCF of \(8a^{2}b\) and \(12ab\) is \(4ab\). \(8a^{2}b \div 4ab = 2a\) and \(12ab \div 4ab = 3\), so the answer is \(4ab(2a + 3)\). \(4(2a^{2}b + 3ab)\) is tempting, but \(ab\) is still common inside the bracket, so 4 is not the HCF.
a.clue: Find the number and the pronumerals that divide both terms.

b.q: Mia takes out the HCF from \(10x^{2} + 15x\). What does she write?
b.why: The HCF of \(10x^{2}\) and \(15x\) is \(5x\). \(10x^{2} \div 5x = 2x\) and \(15x \div 5x = 3\), so the answer is \(5x(2x + 3)\). \(5(2x^{2} + 3x)\) is tempting, but it leaves a common factor of \(x\) inside the bracket, so 5 is not the HCF.
b.clue: Both terms share a number and a pronumeral. Take out both.
